reviews.reason: Both faithfully explain class-conditioned personalization and generated-image prior preservation, report the matched Stable Diffusion comparison, and retain the ablation's fidelity-diversity tradeoff and limitations. A has a narrow explanatory edge: its opening identifies the risk of reproducing only reference views, and it explains why DINO is needed when text-aligned embeddings overlook differences between subjects. B is slightly leaner and clearly interprets the joint comparisons, but gives less motivation for this evaluation contribution. Neither turns qualitative applications into an unrestricted preservation guarantee.

Both accurately explain loss-based filtering against no-call and call-only alternatives, isolate inference-time benefit with the ASDiv disabled control, and bound evaluation, perplexity, scaling, and interactive use. B better connects predictive utility to learned tool selection and explains calendar access as the operative source of DATESET improvement, which the source explicitly supports. A devotes more space to API enumeration, the exact decoding threshold, and another baseline number. Those details are correct, but B's evidence-to-explanation connections make the full contribution easier to follow without overstating superiority to GPT-3 or original GPT-J.

Both give the operative filtering rule, explain what augmented training teaches, and use content-matched and disabled-call controls to distinguish tool access from further training. Both preserve the QA, translation, perplexity, and noninteractive limitations. A usefully states that decoding encourages calls; B adds the source-supported arithmetic comparison with GPT-3 and explicitly confines the scaling sweep to three tools. These are complementary strengths, not a decisive overall difference. Their ASDiv figures match the source's numerical-answer evaluation, and neither claims general mathematical reasoning or universal superiority.

Both capture the personalization mechanism, public evaluation contribution, joint subject/prompt evidence, human preferences, and prior-preservation tradeoff without claiming perfect identity retention. B has a small explanatory advantage: it connects the class prior to variations beyond observed views and states why DINO distinguishes individuals within a class. It also explicitly identifies the shared Stable Diffusion backbone, clarifying the comparison. A's explanation of why both metrics matter is equally sound, and its omissions are not fidelity defects. B's additional causal and evaluation clarity gives it the narrow preference.
